findings.summary: The scope table's left column continues with plain bullets that are not in the table, so in-scope items are split across two forms and the numbers block is a jumble of unlabeled lines.
findings.evidence:
"5M bookings/day
50M MAU
~60/s average
5M / 86,400 s
600/s peak
10x in evening hours
~3,300 req/s
one blockbuster"
findings.fix: Present the scale estimates as a table (Metric | Math | Result) so each number sits beside its label and derivation.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas: the booking and browse availability numbers are split from their reasoning, and the closing callout combines the consistency rule with the availability targets.
findings.evidence: "Browse may be stale; a seat sold twice is never acceptable. That is why browse gets 99.99% and booking only 99.9%."
findings.fix: Split into two one-line bullets: the staleness rule and the availability split.

findings.summary: Read path and write path are listed as two unlabeled node sequences, so a learner cannot tell which chain is which or that they are separate flows.
findings.evidence:
"Client
browse, search
CDN
layout, posters
Redis cache
seat-map status
Read replica
cache miss only
Client
hold, book
Inventory
hold API
Postgres shard
store of record"
findings.fix: Label the two diagrams "Read path" and "Write path" before their nodes, or render them as two separate flows.

findings.summary: The Redis bullet combines two separate uses, and the sizing parenthesis conflicts with the later description of the cache as a bitmap.
findings.evidence: "Redis: hot seat-map cache (200 seats = 25 bytes per show)"
findings.fix: Say "Redis bitmap: 1 bit per seat, 25 bytes per 200-seat show" and keep the hold TTL keys as a separate bullet.

findings.summary: A one-bit-per-seat bitmap cannot encode the three seat states (AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED) that the same page says the map shows.
findings.evidence: "Seat status is one of AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED" vs "Dynamic status: Redis bitmap per show, 1 bit per seat" and "200 seats = 200 bits = 25 bytes per show" (the same 1-bit assumption appears on page 10: "10,000 seats = 1.25 KB")
findings.fix: Say the bit means 'selectable' (1 = available, 0 = held or booked), or use 2 bits per seat (200 seats = 50 bytes, 10,000 seats = 2.5 KB) if the map must tell HELD and BOOKED apart.

findings.summary: The sweeper SQL is shown after a one-line fix but is a long two-statement query that is hard to skim, and the hold tables diagram has dangling "hold_seat / hold" relationship labels with no link meaning.
findings.fix: Replace the stray labels with an explicit relation such as "hold_seat.hold_id → hold.hold_id" and keep the SQL to one statement per idea.

findings.summary: The redis expiry rows are inconsistent: the first bullet says the Redis TTL is only a signal while the row table says the key "expires or deleted", and "{6 seats}" has stray braces.
findings.evidence: "Reserve up to {6 seats} for 8 minutes while the user pays"

findings.summary: The unique constraint is described as both a last guard with no status copy and, on cancel, as requiring deletion of rows, and that second idea sits in the same list as the invariant.
findings.evidence: "On cancel, delete the booking_seat rows so the seat can be sold again"
findings.fix: Move the cancel-deletes-rows note to its own labelled bullet beneath the constraint, since it explains a consequence rather than the invariant.

findings.summary: Two SQL examples are shown with several explanatory bullets before and after each, so the code sits inside a prose block instead of beside a one-line idea.
findings.evidence:
"Optimistic: one conditional UPDATE claims the seats, no lock taken
Rows affected = 0 (or fewer than requested) means you lost the race
Hold is all-or-nothing: on a short count, ROLLBACK"
findings.fix: State the single idea in one line, then show the code with a one-line caption.

findings.summary: The failure flow is drawn as arrow text lines and a bullet pair mixes dedupe by UPDATE with the index backstop.
findings.evidence: "Unique index on gateway_ref is only a backstop: one payment row per ref"
findings.fix: Split the backstop point into its own bullet and draw the expired-hold flow as a labelled diagram.

findings.summary: The cancel flow is labelled "POST cancel to REFUNDED" and the states appear without arrows between nodes, so the sequence order is unclear; the refund policy conflicts with page 11 on boundary wording.
findings.evidence:
"Until 4 h before showtime | 100% of ticket price
Until 2 h before showtime | 50%" vs "4 h or more before | 100%"
findings.fix: Use the same boundary wording on both pages (for example "4 h or more before" and "2 h to 4 h before").

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "inventory", "balances").
findings.evidence: Trade-off: hold TTL length, short TTL frees seats faster but loses slow payers, 8 minutes balances UPI delays with inventory churn
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: A bullet holds more than one idea and the contention line mixes the queue rate with row locking, while the trade-off table's row for shorter TTL repeats a decision as a non-chosen option.
findings.evidence:
"Bound contention with the queue admission rate (about 500 users/s)
Add per-show row locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ordered by seat_id, held a few ms"
findings.fix: Label them as separate mitigations with a one-line reason each.

findings.summary: Page 5 presents the optimistic conditional UPDATE as the main guard, but page 10 recommends pessimistic FOR UPDATE for the hot show without saying it replaces the optimistic path.
findings.evidence: "Add per-show row locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ordered by seat_id, held a few ms"
findings.fix: State that the hot show switches from the optimistic UPDATE to FOR UPDATE, as page 5's guard table says.
